name: Dusty bronze
lede: Dusty bronze is a warm, dark gold-brown, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Kitsurubami, "golden oak," named for a tree's dye rather than the metal its English name suggests.

sections.title: The color of oak dye
sections.body:
Kitsurubami (黄橡) is named in the Wikipedia list of Japan's traditional colors for "golden oak," not for bronze metal [1]. The page gives no further history for the name beyond that literal meaning, and it is undocumented in the sources consulted here [1].

Its nearest named neighbors on file are [[tawny-orange]] and [[ochraceous-tawny]], each 2.7 units off [2], close enough on screen that a tree's dye and a metal both land on the same warm gold-brown.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within six units of this swatch in 1,489 of 23,781 paintings, 6.26 percent, as photographed; looking inside each painting for at least five percent coverage narrows that to 1,194 [3]. That makes it more common than 92 percent of the named colors in our library [3]. It peaks hard in the 1300s, present in 16.3 percent of our 251 paintings from that century, 3.8 times the museums' baseline rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 67 percent of its 1,194 appearances by lightness rank [3].

Pietro Perugino is its most devoted painter on file, present in 7 of his 16 works here, more than four times the baseline rate for the museums that hold them [3]. The earliest match dates to the year 1000, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. It shares canvases with [[indian-yellow|Indian Yellow]] and [[sudan-brown|Sudan Brown]] far more often than chance [3]. These are computed color matches to photographed, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [3].
